title: Fuel in hand
hook: Angiras sends the seeker to a guru with firewood in hand, and that's why students still bring an offering
carry: come to the guru with fuel in hand

segments.voice: Yesterday: plava, the rites as unsteady boats. Good for the lake, not for the ocean. Your line was rites earn a heaven that ends; moksha isn't earned.
screen: `RITES EARN A HEAVEN THAT ENDS; MOKSHA ISN'T EARNED.`

segments.voice: When you show up at someone's house for the first time, you bring something. Because it says: I came on purpose, and I'm not just here to take. The Mundaka itself opens with a visit like that. Shaunaka, a great householder, comes to the sage Angiras the proper way and asks one question: what is it that, once known, makes everything known? Angiras's whole answer is this Upanishad. And right after saying the rites can't carry you across, he says what can: a person, and a bundle of sticks.
screen: `SHAUNAKA COMES TO ANGIRAS.` → `WHAT, ONCE KNOWN, MAKES EVERYTHING KNOWN?` → `WHAT CAN CARRY YOU ACROSS?`

segments.voice: Here's Angiras's verse, Mundaka 1.2.12. Having looked closely at the worlds won by works, a seeker should come to dispassion. The uncreated isn't won by the made. To know that, let him go, fuel in hand, to a teacher who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman. Samitpanih: samit, firewood, the sticks for the sacred fire; pani, hand. Fuel in hand. You met this a few days ago, when the six students came to Pippalada samitpanayah, with fuel in their hands. It's the old sign of a real student: I'll serve, I'll help keep your fire going. And notice the two qualities named for the teacher. Shrotriya: learned in the Veda, someone who has heard and studied. And brahmanishtha: established in Brahman, someone who lives what they know. Both. Then the next verse gives the teacher a duty too. To a student who has come properly, whose mind is calm and settled, the wise teacher should teach, truly, the knowledge by which one knows the imperishable. So the student brings fuel. The teacher brings fire. Both owe something. This is one of Hinduism's oldest teachings: guru and shishya, teacher and student. The deepest knowing passes from a person who lives it, voice to ear. It's why students of music and dance still touch a teacher's feet before a lesson, and why Guru Purnima, a full-moon day, is set aside to honor teachers. The offering isn't a fee. It says: I'm here to serve, and to learn.
screen: `THE MADE CAN'T WIN THE UNMADE.` · `GO TO A TEACHER, FUEL IN HAND.` · `LEARNED, AND ESTABLISHED IN BRAHMAN.` · `GURU AND SHISHYA: BOTH OWE SOMETHING.` · then, large: `SAMITPANI.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that mattered: a parent, a coach, an elder. Then do what many Hindus do for a teacher: fold your hands and bow to them, a pranam, here in your mind. If bowing isn't your way, just say thank you silently. Then ask what fuel you could bring someone teaching you now: patience, attention, showing up.

Brahmanishtha, established in Brahman, one mark of a true teacher. The Mundaka's instruction: go, fuel in hand, to one who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman, who then must teach truly.
Your line: come to the guru with fuel in hand. Tomorrow, the fire that fuel was for. Day four hundred fourteen, done.

howItsDone: In many Hindu traditions students approach a teacher with an offering and study in the guru-shishya relationship; Guru Purnima, on the full moon of Ashadha, is a day many set aside to honor their teachers.
